entries.title: Built a Gmail pipeline toolkit to clean up my own inbox
entries.note: A command-line pipeline that sorts, labels and structures a Gmail account, built because doing it by hand was not going to happen. It needs real setup and it is not for non-technical users; the README is the honest version. Verify what it does before pointing it at your mail, and keep sensitive data out of it.
entries.obstacle: A backlog of unread mail large enough that manual triage was not a plan, only a wish.
entries.learning: The reason was half organisation and half curiosity, and both were served. The inbox is structured now and I understand the API I was avoiding.

entries.title: Twenty episodes published
entries.note: Eighteen on databases, one on LLM cost, one long-form essay. Every one of them something I had to understand properly first.
entries.learning: Publishing is the deadline that makes the learning real.

entries.title: Attended The Autonomous AI Product Engineer
entries.note: A Shunnek Labs session on where the product engineer role goes when the agent does the typing.

entries.title: Talked with Ariful Jannat Arif about what makes software good
entries.note: Discussed the traits of good software, the metrics behind it, and the KPIs that matter on Google Play and the App Store.
entries.learning: What you measure on the store is what the store rewards. Know the KPIs before you ship.

entries.title: Gave the channel a curriculum
entries.note: Series codes and an append-only episode register, so a viewer who liked one video can find the next three. Numbered in course order, never renumbered once public.
entries.learning: A channel becomes a course the moment the order means something.

entries.title: Talked with Saiful Islam about the founder journey
entries.note: Discussed the founder journey, the app business, what a product-based company looks like from the inside, the traits of a great product, and how to approach all of it.
entries.learning: Great products come from clear traits and a deliberate approach, not luck.

entries.title: Shipped the product I had been building, on Google Play
entries.note: The second app on Google Play, six weeks after the first, and the one the work was actually about. Store listing, screenshots and all -- from a blank Flutter project to a shipping product in a few months.
entries.obstacle: Everything that has to be true before a store accepts an app, all at once.
entries.learning: Shipping is a checklist, not a feeling.

entries.title: Production infrastructure live for the product
entries.note: Stood up the production environment for the product I had been building from zero: servers, database, deploy path and readiness checks, all verified end to end. Live the day before the app reached Google Play.

entries.title: Wrote "Computer Science Didn't Stop Being Valuable"
entries.note: The full title is "Computer Science Didn't Stop Being Valuable. The Order You Learn It In Broke." The argument is that the fundamentals did not lose their worth -- the sequence people are taught them in stopped matching the way software is now built.

entries.title: Talked with Hasanuzzaman Shamim about how AI is reshaping the industry
entries.note: Discussed AI in the tech industry as a whole: how it is changing, how it is affecting us, and how we are coping with it.
entries.learning: Meetups like this exist to widen the picture. Someone else's vantage point is the cheapest upgrade there is.

entries.title: Upgraded how theainativeengineer ships
entries.note: A pipeline that turns one idea into a narrated, animated reel, gated at every step, with one promise behind it: do not explain the system, make you watch it run.
entries.obstacle: Most tech content tells you what to type. Almost nothing shows what actually happens underneath.
entries.learning: Systems intuition is usually earned from outages. It can be compressed.

entries.title: The trail begins
entries.note: Started logging growth publicly: wins, obstacles, and lessons, one day at a time.
entries.learning: Consistency compounds. The tree only grows if you feed it.

entries.title: Built agent-auto-start, so a session limit stops costing me the thread
entries.note: A small tool that restarts Claude automatically when a session limit has reset, instead of leaving the work parked until I notice.
entries.learning: The interruptions that cost most are not the long ones, they are the ones that need you present to clear them.

entries.title: First app on Google Play
entries.note: Pushed to Google Play at 07:28 on 26 June 2026. A different product from the one that followed in July, smaller in scope, and it went into production and stayed there.
entries.obstacle: Everything a store requires before it will take an app at all -- signing, review, listing, policy -- learned on the way through rather than in advance.
entries.learning: The first release teaches you the pipeline, not the product. Every app after this one costs a fraction of what this one did, and that saving is the real output.

entries.title: Built a local-only iPhone storage inspector
entries.note: Reads real storage data from a connected iPhone over USB and explains where the space went, including the hidden purgeable cache. Nothing leaves the machine.
entries.learning: People distrust cleanup tools for good reason. Reading every line yourself is the feature.

entries.title: Shipped CityPhone 28, a bilingual site for a phone-repair shop
entries.note: FR/EN for a repair shop in Chartres: a live open and closed status in Paris time, GDPR-compliant map consent, LocalBusiness structured data and per-locale hreflang.

entries.title: Built Shamba Cast, weather advice for smallholder farmers
entries.note: Turns a raw forecast into the decisions a farmer actually makes, when to plant, spray and harvest, and delivers it to a feature phone over SMS and USSD with no internet needed.
entries.learning: The hardest constraint was not the forecast. It was the phone on the other end.

entries.title: Started posting on X in the open
entries.note: Began using X actively on 3 June 2026 -- working in public rather than posting finished things.

entries.title: Contributed to serious-oj, a production online judge
entries.note: A judge for ACM and OI style contests, run by Eluminatis of LU and built on a fork of vijos. I contributed to the platform rather than authoring it.
entries.learning: Working inside somebody else's architecture is a different skill from starting your own.

entries.title: Built a grounded legal-drafting system for an AI engineer interview
entries.note: A three-day take-home: retrieval-grounded legal drafting, where every generated clause has to be traceable to a source document rather than asserted. One of the three days went on a platform I had never used before.
entries.obstacle: Two of the three days were spent inside a domain I had never worked in -- legal drafting -- and one of those on unfamiliar tooling. The interview then pressed on architecture rather than output: why Postgres for the vector store instead of FAISS or a dedicated vector database, and a run of retrieval questions behind it.
entries.learning: Choosing Postgres was defensible and I could not defend it fast enough. Knowing why you did not pick the obvious tool is a separate piece of preparation from building the thing, and it is the piece that gets tested. No update came afterwards.

entries.title: Went to a WordPress meetup to watch another domain handle the AI transition
entries.note: A WordPress community meetup hosted at AuthLab in Sylhet. I am not a WordPress developer and did not go to become one. I went to hear how an ecosystem I have no stake in is absorbing AI -- what its practitioners are actually changing, and how the teams around them are reorganising to match.
entries.learning: The transition looks different from inside a domain that is not yours, and that is the only place you can see your own assumptions. The questions people were asking were not the ones I would have predicted from outside.

entries.title: TestForge, a mutation-driven test-backfill agent
entries.note: An autonomous agent that writes pytest suites which kill surviving mutants, not just hit coverage. Built for the Hourglass AI Agent Challenge.
entries.learning: Coverage is a proxy. Killing mutants is the thing coverage was trying to measure.

entries.title: Started theainativeengineer
entries.note: Began posting regularly on Instagram, Facebook and YouTube: everything I learn, turned into short explainers for engineers.
entries.learning: A channel is a curriculum in public. Consistency, not virality, is the job.

entries.title: Delivered Sushi Lab, a solo end-to-end build
entries.note: A production bilingual ordering and marketing platform for a Japanese restaurant in Chartres, France: Next.js 16, React 19, server actions, translated URL segments and locale-aware checkout.
entries.learning: One person can own a whole product now. The constraint moved from hands to judgment.

entries.title: Closed my chapter at LII Lab after 1,276 days
entries.note: Joined on 1 November 2022, before graduating, and left on 30 April 2026 -- three and a half years. I was one of the core engineers behind OnePTE and OneIELTS, in the room from the earliest product conversations through to the systems running in production today: requirements into system design, backend build, deployment, monitoring, production debugging, and mentoring the juniors who came after me.
entries.obstacle: Leaving the place and people where I grew from graduate to senior engineer.
entries.learning: The visible output is a contribution graph. The rest of it does not render: systems staying up, exams completing, payments clearing, releases going out, teammates getting better. End-to-end ownership is mostly the invisible half.
entries.outcome: 1,276 days; 93+ production releases across Android, iOS and web

entries.title: Wrote "AI Tools Are The New Frameworks"
entries.note: An argument that AI tools now occupy the position frameworks used to: the layer you choose early, that quietly decides how you work for years afterwards.

entries.title: Sat a recorded video interview for an engineering role
entries.note: A one-way recorded interview, submitted 20 February 2026 at 15:17.
entries.learning: A recorded interview is a different skill from a conversation. There is nobody to read, so you lose the one signal that tells you whether to go deeper or move on.

entries.title: Walked at my convocation, three years after finishing
entries.note: Tassel on the left. The degree was finished in March 2023; the ceremony was January 2026. Four years of it, 2018 to 2023, and the people were the part worth showing up for.
entries.outcome: B.Sc. in Computer Science and Engineering

entries.title: Judged the hackathon at NEUB ICT Fest
entries.note: A one-problem hackathon: automate the end to end vaccination process for Bangladesh, from citizen registration and appointment scheduling through to stock tracking and wastage reporting. I scored teams on what they built and how they explained it.
entries.learning: Judging teaches you what a demo actually has to prove in five minutes.

entries.title: Three years at LII Lab
entries.note: Three years with the same team, on the same two products. Long enough to maintain what I had built, which is the part of the job that teaches you what you got wrong.
entries.learning: Three years in one place is where you meet your own decisions again. Nothing tells you the cost of a shortcut like having to live beside it.

entries.title: Taught CV building and interview preparation at CPS Academy
entries.note: A two-hour evening session: why a CV matters, how to build one that survives a skim, how to prepare for interviews, and how to handle questions without performing. Slides published afterwards.
entries.learning: Most people preparing for interviews are not under-skilled, they are under-narrated. The session that helps is the one about how to say what you already did.

entries.title: Took OneIELTS multi-tenant so it could sell to institutes
entries.note: Rebuilt OneIELTS as a B2B product for IELTS institutes: tenant architecture, data isolation, a large dataset migration, strict per-tenant access control, and white-label support in the web app.
entries.obstacle: Nobody on the team had built a SaaS product before, and every existing app and website user had to go through the migration without noticing it happened.
entries.learning: Multi-tenancy is decided once, at the isolation boundary, and every other decision follows from it. Getting that one right is most of the work; getting it wrong is a rewrite.
entries.outcome: Shipped, zero disruption to existing users

entries.title: Interviewed candidates for the backend and mobile teams
entries.note: Sat on the other side of the table at LII Lab, running technical interviews for backend and mobile engineering roles.
entries.obstacle: Judging someone's ability in an hour, knowing how little an hour shows.
entries.learning: Running interviews teaches you more about interviews than sitting them does. You stop performing and start listening for how someone thinks.

entries.title: Promoted to Senior Software Engineer
entries.note: Led backend engineering across two AI-powered English test-prep platforms: architecture, mentoring, and production releases.
entries.learning: Seniority is responsibility for other people's growth, and code comes second.

entries.title: Judged and set problems for LU IUJPC: Sylhet Division 2024
entries.note: Inter-university junior programming contest for the Sylhet division. Thirty-five teams competed; the field solved 6 of the 11 problems, which is roughly the spread a problem set is aiming for. Hosted on SeriousOJ.
entries.learning: A problem set is judged by its distribution, not by its hardest problem. Eleven problems where the field clears six is a set that separated people instead of just defeating them.

entries.title: Reconnected with LU CSE alumni across six batches
entries.note: An evening with Leading University CSE alumni spanning the 4th batch through the 53rd, arranged through the alumni association. I first met one of them two years earlier at a university webinar, while I was Chair of the IEEE Computer Society chapter.
entries.learning: A department's real output is not its curriculum, it is a network that keeps answering thirty batches later.

entries.title: Judged and set problems for the Intra IEEE Programming Contest
entries.note: Judge and problem setter for the intra-university programming contest at Leading University, run by the IEEE Computer Society LU SB Chapter.
entries.org: IEEE Computer Society LU SB Chapter

entries.title: Set two contests for the IEEE CS chapter on short notice
entries.note: Two contests for chapter members, junior and senior category, eight problems each, two hours, hosted on HackerRank. Organised and problem-set by the judge panel from scratch.
entries.obstacle: The whole thing came together on short notice -- the panel had to organise the event and author sixteen problems in the time available.
entries.org: IEEE Computer Society LU SB Chapter

entries.title: Went to WordCamp Sylhet to look outside my own domain
entries.note: Conference day at the SUST central auditorium. First WordCamp, and deliberately nothing to do with backend engineering -- I went to see how a different discipline organises itself.
entries.learning: Worth it, and I would go again. The sessions were cut short by the schedule, the last panel most of all, which is its own lesson about running an event: the programme is a budget, and the panel is what gets spent.

entries.title: Champion at the National Hackathon, LU CSE Carnival
entries.note: My first hackathon, and we won it. Two people, one build, top spot at the National Hackathon of LU CSE Carnival Season 2.

entries.title: Wrote up how to recover deleted local commits in Git
entries.note: A step-by-step piece on getting commits back after they have been deleted locally -- reflog, and the fact that Git almost never actually loses anything you committed.
entries.learning: The article people needed was not the clever one. It was the one written the day I needed it myself.

entries.title: IEEE Outstanding Leadership Volunteer Award
entries.note: Outstanding Leadership Volunteer Award, for serving the IEEE Computer Society LU SB Chapter as Chair on the 2022-23 steering committee.

entries.title: Handed the chapter over through the first election in the university's history
entries.note: As Chair, I did not appoint a successor. The executive committee was elected -- the first committee at Leading University ever chosen by a vote rather than by handover.
entries.learning: The real test of founding something is whether it survives you leaving. An election is the only handover that proves it can.
entries.org: IEEE Computer Society LU SB Chapter

entries.title: Judged a school science fair
entries.note: Judged the science fair at Shahjalal Jameya Islamiya Kamil Madrasha in Pathantula, Sylhet, brought in through the IEEE Computer Society LU SB Chapter's STEM outreach.
entries.learning: First time questioning rather than presenting. Asking a fifteen-year-old why their project works, without leading them to the answer, is a harder interview technique than any I had used.

entries.title: Graduated with a B.Sc. in Computer Science and Engineering
entries.note: Four years, finished officially in December 2022, with the final-year project defence following in March 2023. I had been at LII Lab for two months by the time the degree completed.

entries.title: Joined LII Lab as a Software Engineer
entries.note: Built the OnePTE Flutter app from day one and the Django backend powering AI scoring.
entries.obstacle: Owning a full product stack for the first time, while still finishing my degree.
entries.learning: Ship, observe, improve. Ownership is the fastest teacher.

entries.title: Completed CLAP, the IEEE Region 10 leadership programme
entries.note: Shortlisted for the Career and Leadership Aid Program 2022, run by IEEE Young Professionals across Region 10. Two days, run in clusters, with people from across the region.
entries.learning: The value was not the curriculum. It was two days in a room with people solving the same problems in countries that resource them completely differently.

entries.title: Runner-up in Bangladesh at IEEEXtreme 16.0
entries.note: Global rank 149 with Team LazySquad. Twenty-four hours of non-stop problem solving.

entries.title: Projecto, my final-year project
entries.note: A multi-role Django app for university project proposals: students, supervisors and admins, with PDF and CSV export and scheduled background jobs.

entries.title: Published my online-judge solution archive
entries.note: Years of accepted solutions, in the open.

entries.title: Set problems for a contest for the first time
entries.note: The first time a problem I authored went in front of contestants rather than the other way round.
entries.obstacle: Right up to the moment the contest started I could not tell whether my problem was too easy or about right. There is no way to test that on yourself -- you already know the answer.
entries.learning: Setting a problem is a calibration skill, not a difficulty skill. Writing something hard is easy; writing something that separates a field is not.

entries.title: Organized the Flutter app development bootcamp
entries.note: Fourteen weeks teaching juniors to ship a mobile app, while shipping one myself at work.

entries.title: Ranked 85th of 1,747 teams at the ICPC Dhaka Regional Online Preliminary
entries.note: The 2021 season preliminary, hosted by BUBT. Team LU_sTrongWill.

entries.title: Cleared the Google Code Jam qualification round again
entries.note: 44 points in the 2022 global qualifier, two points better than 2020.

entries.title: Co-founded and chaired the IEEE Computer Society LU Student Branch Chapter
entries.note: Built the chapter from nothing, ran technical events with industry speakers, and grew membership by more than 20%.
entries.obstacle: Starting a chapter means proving there is demand before anyone believes you.
entries.learning: A community is not an audience. It is a group of people who show up for each other.

entries.title: Organized the Data Communications and Industrial Networking Bootcamp
entries.note: Twelve weeks of hands-on training for juniors.

entries.title: Elected Joint General Secretary of the LU Sports Club
entries.note: Ran inter-department tournaments and university sporting events for a year.
entries.learning: Running an event is the same skill as running a release. Different room.

entries.title: Took responsibility as ACM Coordinator at the LU Computer Club
entries.note: Ran peer-to-peer DSA sessions and mentored juniors through Codeforces, CodeChef and LightOJ.
entries.learning: Teaching a thing is the fastest way to truly learn it.

entries.title: Champion at LU TechStorm 4
entries.note: First place on home ground, with Team Catapult.

entries.title: HomeHunt, my third-year Flutter project
entries.note: A rental-listing app, and the first time I shipped something with a real UI.

entries.title: IEEEXtreme 15.0
entries.note: The second twenty-four hour marathon. Country rank 6, global rank 164, with Team SchrodenBug.

entries.title: Organized the LU Research Bootcamp 2021
entries.note: The first research bootcamp of its kind in Bangladesh, run by the IEEE Computer Society LU SB Chapter. Participants came from twelve different universities, and registrations reached beyond the country into China and India.
entries.outcome: Twelve universities; participants from three countries

entries.note: Six weeks learning how research actually gets done before helping run it.
entries.learning: Learn the thing first. Then you have earned the right to organize it.

entries.title: Ranked 51st at the ICPC Dhaka Regional 2020 Main Round
entries.note: The regional main round, hosted by CSE, University of Dhaka. Team LU_SchrodenBug.
entries.learning: Hard problems bend to consistent practice.

entries.title: Reached Expert on Codeforces
entries.note: Crossed 1600 after Codeforces Round 714, Division 2. Expert is the rating band where the problems stop rewarding pattern-matching and start requiring a proof before you type.
entries.obstacle: The rating had sat one band below for a long time before this contest moved it.

entries.title: Peak CodeChef rating of 1965
entries.note: January Cook-Off 2021, Division 2. Global rank 127, and the highest rating I reached on CodeChef.

entries.title: IEEEXtreme 14.0, the 24-hour global marathon
entries.note: Twenty-four hours without stopping. Country rank 9, global rank 465, with Team LURisingStar.

entries.title: Started a public algorithm handbook
entries.note: Everything I was learning about data structures, written down where anyone could read it.
entries.learning: Writing it down is how you find out whether you understood it.

entries.title: Cleared the Google Code Jam qualification round
entries.note: 42 points in the 2020 global qualifier.

entries.title: Ranked 5th at the LU Intra University Programming Contest
entries.note: Team LU_Untitled. Early days, and the first time the practice showed on a scoreboard.

entries.title: Participated in Computenigma, a programming contest at BAIUST
entries.note: A contest at another university, against people who had never seen us before.

entries.title: Participated in the LU CSE Carnival programming contest
entries.note: Home ground, and the first year of competing seriously.

entries.title: Honorable Mention at the ICPC Asia Dhaka Regional Online Preliminary
entries.note: Representing Leading University in the online preliminary. The certificate was issued later that September.
entries.learning: Hard problems bend to consistent practice.

entries.title: First inter-university contest: LICT SUST TechFest
entries.note: Two days at SUST with Team LU-Newbies2. The name was honest.
entries.learning: You do not find out where the bar is by reading about it.

entries.title: Started a B.Sc. in Computer Science and Engineering
entries.note: Four years of fundamentals, contests, and late nights begin.

entries.title: Completed HSC in Science at Beanibazar Govt. College
entries.note: Higher Secondary Certificate. Chose science, and the path toward engineering.

entries.title: Completed SSC at Purba Muria High School
entries.note: Secondary School Certificate, Sylhet. The first checkpoint.

profile.name: Mazharul Islam
profile.bio: Building products and sharing what I learn along the way. Backend, frontend, mobile, infrastructure, DevOps, ML - all of it, because agents made the parts I used to hand off cheap enough to keep. One person can hold a whole product now. Still working out what that changes, which is turning out to be most of the job.
profile.creed_belief: The only difference between the success you see and where I stand today is time.
profile.creed_practice: Just keep trying to become better everyday. That's all.

experience.summary: Led backend engineering for OneIELTS and OnePTE, AI-powered English test preparation platforms.
bullets: Architected a multi-tenant SaaS backend with django-multitenant: full data isolation, custom domain routing, per-tenant scoring config and feature flags.
Designed a QTI 3.0-compliant exam engine supporting 100+ question types across IELTS Academic and General, with XML parsing, interaction routing, and strategy-pattern band-score normalization.
Built a real-time speech evaluation pipeline integrating speech recognition, pronunciation assessment and NLP processing, with end-to-end scoring in under 15 seconds.
Engineered multi-gateway payment infrastructure across 5 providers, with subscription lifecycle management and webhook idempotency.
Built the Studio API layer for the moderator platform: content authoring, expert evaluation queue, exam rejudge pipelines, and KPI analytics.
Set up production observability with Prometheus and Grafana: health monitoring, per-API latency instrumentation, and alerting.
Mentored junior engineers through code reviews, PR feedback, and architectural walkthroughs.

experience.summary: Full-stack ownership of OnePTE: designed and shipped the Flutter app from day one and built the Django AI scoring backend.
bullets: Designed and built the Flutter cross-platform app from scratch: all four PTE modules with 20+ task types, audio recording, and timer management.
Built a task-group-based mock test engine with modular exam templates, configurable time allocations, automated question progression, and multi-dimensional score breakdowns.
Engineered the AI scoring backend for spoken and written tasks using speech recognition, pronunciation assessment and NLP processing for multi-trait evaluation.
Integrated subscription billing across 4 platforms with webhook handling, transaction deduplication, and in-app purchase verification.
Built the Django admin and private API for content moderation, question bank management, subscription analytics with regional reporting, and user acquisition dashboards.
Led 93+ production releases across Android, iOS and Web; managed release pipelines, Firebase config, and CI/CD across all channels.

projects.name: OneIELTS

Architected the backend from zero, including a QTI 3.0 question engine, automated scoring across all four skill areas, multi-gateway payment infrastructure, and a production observability stack.

Internal Studio API for the moderator platform: authoring, expert evaluation queue, rejudge pipelines and KPI analytics
Five payment gateways with subscription lifecycle management and idempotent webhook processing
Production observability, device-restricted JWT auth, and GDPR-compliant account deletion

Practice and mock test system covering all four modules with 20+ task types and automated question progression
Real-time AI scoring for spoken and written submissions, delivering results within 10 to 15 seconds
Multi-platform billing with real-time payment webhooks, transaction deduplication and in-app purchase verification
Django admin and private API for content moderation, exam management, subscription analytics and acquisition dashboards
Extended the app to Flutter Web with full responsive desktop implementations

Triple-channel notifications for every order, reservation and contact submission, dispatched in parallel with strict cross-channel data parity
AI-discoverable SEO: JSON-LD, dynamic sitemap, dynamic OG images, per-locale canonical and hreflang, and llms.txt
GA4 ecommerce funnel plus reservation, contact, language-switch and Web Vitals events

PDF and CSV export for project reports
Background job service for scheduled operations
